lines.text: Run the exact same equality filter against the exact same table, two different ways.
With no index at all, over ten thousand buffers get touched to answer it.
With one tiny summary index instead, only fifteen do.
An ordinary tree-shaped index stores one entry for every single row it covers, no matter how many rows that is.
Could an index that stores nothing at all per row still manage to help answer a query?
Yes — a much coarser summary can still rule out most of the table at once.
A summary covering many rows together can still prove that an entire group of them cannot possibly match, which is exactly the mechanism this topic measures directly.
This kind of index keeps one summary for each group of physically neighboring pages, instead of one entry per row.
For a column with a natural order, that summary is simply the smallest and largest value seen anywhere inside that whole group.
One compact fact, standing in for every row the group actually contains.
Build that kind of index on this column, and measure its size directly.
It comes out to a few dozen kilobytes. An ordinary tree-shaped index over the identical column comes out to several megabytes instead.
Hundreds of times larger, for storing the exact same column, the exact same data.
A summary this coarse only ever rules out a whole group of rows at once, never a single row by itself.
Does that still work no matter how a column's values happen to be arranged inside the table, or does something about the data have to be true first?

tolerated.line: A summary this coarse only ever rules out a whole group of rows at once, never a single row by itself.

lines.text: It only helps once a group's rows genuinely share values that are close together.
Whether that holds at all is a real property of how the data sits physically in the table, and this topic measures both sides of that directly.
A group's own summary is only a useful shortcut if that group's rows are genuinely clustered together by value.
In other words, the column has to be well matched to the physical order the rows actually sit in.
Without that match, a compact summary has nothing meaningful left to summarize.
Pick a column that is genuinely well matched to row order, and measure the same equality filter again.
Buffers drop all the way back down to that same small handful, and the whole query finishes in a tiny fraction of a millisecond.
Hundreds of times faster than touching the table with no index at all.
Now take the exact same kind of index, but on a column whose values are scattered randomly across the table instead.
Does it still help at all?
No — once values are scattered, almost every group ends up containing nearly the full spread of them.
A summary covering a group that already contains everything has nothing left to rule out.
Measure that same scattered-column case directly.
The number of buffers touched comes out essentially the same as touching the table with no index at all.
And once the extra checking work this index still has to do gets counted, it actually finishes slightly slower than skipping the index entirely.
A group's own summary can be perfectly consistent with a filter without every single row inside that group actually matching it.
So what has to happen, then, to those rows before they can be trusted as real matches?
Every row inside a matching group still has to be checked individually before being trusted.
The summary only proves a group might contain a real match, never that every row inside it already is one.
A matching group hands back every single row it contains as a mere candidate, nothing more.
The engine running the query then checks each candidate against the real filter on its own, one at a time.
Whatever doesn't genuinely match gets thrown away right there — this kind of index gives up precision by design, in exchange for its own tiny size.
A columnar file format keeps this exact same trick at its own layer, one level removed from a database engine entirely.
Each chunk of rows inside such a file carries its own smallest and largest value, read before a single row inside that chunk ever gets decoded.
The exact same shortcut, just applied to a file instead of a table.
A cloud warehouse carries this same idea even further, automatically, for every table it stores.
Each small chunk of a table keeps the range of values for every one of its own columns, and an entire chunk gets skipped the moment that range cannot possibly match.
Different storage layer, same underlying principle this whole topic has been measuring directly.
A summary this coarse costs almost nothing to store, next to an ordinary tree-shaped index over the same column.
It only earns that advantage once a column's values genuinely line up with how the table is physically laid out.
And even then, every row a matching group returns still gets individually checked before it counts as a real answer.

tolerated.line: A summary this coarse costs almost nothing to store, next to an ordinary tree-shaped index over the same column.

lines.text: A table is split into five hundred physical groups of rows. Every row was loaded in strict order by date, and a query filters on exactly one date, which only ever appears inside a single one of those groups.
How many of those groups, though, actually need to be checked?
Just one — every other group gets ruled out purely by its own summary.
With the data this strictly ordered, only the single group whose own summary could possibly contain that date needs any checking done on it at all.
